lead: An ILS lets an aircraft fly a straight descent to a runway even when the runway is not in sight. It broadcasts two radio beams: one tells the aircraft whether it is left or right of the centreline, the other whether it is above or below the correct slope. The crew follows two needles on the flight display. ILS is the world's standard precision approach aid; MLS was designed to remove its siting limits, and satellite augmentation is now replacing both.
prereq: You need 5.1 for lines of position and 5.2 for the point-source idea and DME ranging.

blocks.text: ILS is a point-source aid: the runway-end equipment is the known point, and the aircraft measures angles from it. Two separate transmitters define the two angles. The localizer, at the far end of the runway, works in the VHF band 108–112 MHz. It has 40 channels, spaced 50 kHz, using the odd-tenth pattern (108.10, 108.15, 108.30, 108.35 MHz and so on). It defines the runway centreline: fly with zero left-right deviation and you track the centreline. The glideslope transmitter, beside the touchdown zone, works in the UHF band 329.15–335 MHz. Its 40 channels are paired with the localizer channels, spaced 150 kHz apart, so selecting one ILS frequency tunes both receivers. It defines the descent angle, usually 3° to the runway. Range comes from marker beacons at 75 MHz — outer, middle and inner — or from a DME paired with the ILS. Approach lighting adds the final visual segment. Full-scale needle deflection is 2.5° each side of the localizer centreline and 0.7° total for the glideslope, that is ±0.35°.

Both transmitters send an amplitude-modulated carrier. The modulation is at 90 Hz and 150 Hz. The receiver separates the two tones and compares their depths: m90 and m150, each a fraction from 0 to 1. On the localizer, 90 Hz is stronger to the left of the centreline and 150 Hz is stronger to the right. On the glideslope, 150 Hz is stronger above the path and 90 Hz is stronger below. Equal depths give DDM = 0, the on-path condition. Full-scale DDM is 0.155 on the localizer and 0.175 on the glideslope; at full scale the needle is at the edge of its scale. The pilot flies to keep both needles centred. A category I approach needs a decision height of 60 m (200 ft) and runway visual range of 550 m. CAT II needs 30 m (100 ft) and 300 m. CAT IIIA goes below 30 m or has no decision height and needs 200 m. IIIB needs 50 m. IIIC has no limits. The categories describe the whole system — aircraft, crew and ground equipment — not the receiver alone.

blocks.where: m<sub>150</sub> and m<sub>90</sub> are the modulation depths at 150 Hz and 90 Hz, each from 0 to 1. Positive DDM means 150 Hz is stronger.

blocks.text: MLS was designed to overcome ILS limits. It works at about 5 GHz, 5031–5091 MHz, with 200 channels. Instead of a steady beam whose modulation depth is measured, MLS uses a time-referenced scanning beam: a narrow beam sweeps across the approach sector, and the receiver times the pass. Azimuth coverage is about ±60° and elevation coverage 0–20°. That wide sector allows curved and segmented approaches, not just a straight line. At 5 GHz the site is much less sensitive to buildings, terrain and ground reflections, and the antenna is small. MLS is paired with DME-P for precise range. ILS remains cheaper and is fitted at most runways. MLS saw limited civil uptake because ILS was already installed and satellite methods arrived. The modern replacement is satellite augmentation: GBAS corrects GPS locally for precision approach, and SBAS provides a wide-area correction. These are covered in 5.6.

figure.caption: The localizer and glideslope are separate receiver chains. Each turns a 90 Hz versus 150 Hz modulation difference into one needle on the primary flight display.

spec.title: Two beams, two deviations
spec.aria: Two parallel receiver chains, one for the localizer and one for the glideslope, each turning a modulation difference into a needle deflection on the same display.

examples.question: An aircraft is on a 3° ILS glide path and the DME reads 5.0 nm to the threshold. (a) What height should the aircraft be at? (b) The glideslope receiver measures a DDM of 0.05 with 150 Hz stronger. The glideslope full-scale DDM is 0.175 at 0.35°. How far off path is the aircraft, and on which side?
steps: Convert range to feet: 1 nm = 6076 ft, so 5.0 nm = 5.0 × 6076 = 30,380 ft.
Height = range × tan(3°). tan 3° = 0.05241. Height = 30,380 × 0.05241 = 1592 ft. Rounded, 1590 ft, or about 318 ft per nm.
Convert DDM to a fraction of full scale: fraction = 0.05 ÷ 0.175 = 0.2857.
Full-scale angle is 0.35°, so angular deviation = 0.2857 × 0.35° = 0.100°. Rounded, 0.10°.
150 Hz stronger means above the path on the glideslope, so the aircraft is above the 3° path.
examples.answer: The aircraft should be at about 1592 ft (roughly 1590 ft, or 318 ft per nm); it is 0.10° above the 3° path.
examples.check:
import math
r_nm = 5.0
r_ft = r_nm * 6076
h = r_ft * math.tan(math.radians(3))
print(round(h))
ddm = 0.05
fs_ddm = 0.175
fs_angle = 0.35
dev = (ddm / fs_ddm) * fs_angle
print(round(dev, 2))

traps: Do not carry the localizer sense across to the glideslope: on the localizer 90 Hz is left and 150 Hz is right; on the glideslope 150 Hz is above and 90 Hz is below.
Do not swap the bands: localizer 108–112 MHz VHF, glideslope 329.15–335 MHz UHF.
Full-scale deflection is 2.5° each side of the localizer centreline, but 0.7° total (±0.35°) on the glideslope.
CAT IIIA is either below 30 m or no decision height; only IIIC has no limits at all.
The marker beacon is at 75 MHz and gives range, not guidance; it does not define the centreline or slope.

quiz.q: State the frequency band and channel spacing of the ILS localizer and glideslope.
quiz.a: Localizer: 108–112 MHz VHF, 40 channels at 50 kHz spacing in the odd-tenth pattern. Glideslope: 329.15–335 MHz UHF, 40 paired channels at 150 kHz spacing.

quiz.q: Why does an ILS receiver use modulation depth rather than received signal strength to find the deviation?
quiz.a: Signal strength falls with range and changes with rain, terrain and antenna pattern. The ratio of 90 Hz to 150 Hz depth is set by the angle from the beam centre and is not affected by overall strength, so it gives a stable deviation.

quiz.q: Localizer DDM is 0.08 with 90 Hz stronger. Full-scale DDM is 0.155 at 2.5°. Find the angular deviation and side.
quiz.a: Fraction = 0.08 ÷ 0.155 = 0.516. Angle = 0.516 × 2.5° = 1.29°. 90 Hz stronger means left of the centreline.

quiz.q: Give two reasons MLS is less site-sensitive than ILS.
quiz.a: It uses a narrow scanning beam at about 5 GHz, so it is less affected by ground reflections and buildings. The receiver measures time of beam passage, not amplitude over a broad beam, and the wide sector allows siting away from obstructions.

quiz.q: Give the decision height and RVR for CAT I and CAT II ILS.
quiz.a: CAT I: decision height 60 m (200 ft), RVR 550 m. CAT II: decision height 30 m (100 ft), RVR 300 m.

quiz.q: Why is DME often paired with ILS instead of marker beacons?
quiz.a: DME gives continuous range to the threshold, so the crew can cross-check height and distance all the way down. Markers give only three discrete fixes and can be missed.

quiz.q: An aircraft is on a 3° path at 2000 ft. What DME range should it read on flat ground?

beyond: Not for the exam. In service, ILS performance is checked by flight inspection, and GBAS is being introduced at major airports for precision approaches with fewer ground antennas. MLS saw limited civil uptake, but its scanning-beam principle appears in millimetre-wave landing sensors and in some military systems. Research now looks at GNSS-based autoland with integrity monitoring and at using the aircraft's own multi-sensor navigation to fly curved approaches. Search for 'GBAS CAT III', 'ILS flight inspection' and 'MLS scanning beam' if you want the operational detail.
